title: The Quad Reassessed: Key Takeaways
text:
The Quad Reassessed: Key Takeaways

Photo by Julia Demaree Nikhinson / POOL / AFP via Getty Images

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), comprising the United States, Japan, India, and Australia, has entered a defining period. The absence of a leaders’ summit thus far, and the possibility of reduced U.S. leadership engagement as well as a softer approach to China suggest that the Quad is foundering. Yet the grouping has maintained momentum at the ministerial level, meeting twice in 2026: first in New Delhi in May and again in July on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Manila.Over the past year, and through the course of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Cementing the Quad in the Indo-Pacific project, the Quad has appeared increasingly focused on advancing a pragmatic, streamlined agenda. At the same time, its prospects have become more closely intertwined with the state of Washington’s bilateral relationships with its partners, particularly India. Critical minerals, economic and energy security, maritime security, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) have emerged as core pillars of cooperation, but those efforts are overshadowed by the state of U.S. relations with the other capitals.To better understand how regional perceptions of the Quad have evolved over the past year, the project team convened a group of experts with a virtual roundtable and an in-person panel to assess the significance of its ministerial-level progress and consider its future engagement across the Indo-Pacific, including in South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands. Several key takeaways emerged.1. The absence of a leaders’ summit does not, in itself, diminish the Quad’s value.The failure to convene a leaders’ summit over the past year has raised questions about the Quad’s political momentum, but it does not necessarily signal institutional decline. However, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his recent trip to India, confirmed that a Quad leaders’ summit would take place on the sidelines of the November 2026 ASEAN Summit in Manila.In the meantime, regular ministerial engagement has kept the grouping active so far and may, in some areas, offer a more effective route to translating shared ambitions into practical cooperation. In fact, to firm up the leadership summit agenda, the Quad foreign ministers are reconvening on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers meeting in Atlanta at the end of October.Maritime security provides a case in point. The expansion of the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA), including through the recently launched Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration (IPMSC), points to opportunities for deeper operational coordination. India is also set to host the next edition of the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, intended to strengthen interoperability and knowledge-sharing.The policy imperative is to ensure that ministerial engagement produces measurable outcomes. A leaders’ meeting can provide political direction, but sustained implementation is what gives the Quad its practical value.2. The U.S.-India relationship remains the Quad’s most consequential bilateral constraint.Strains in U.S.-India relations have become a significant challenge for the grouping. Trade negotiations have remained tenuous, with talks reaching a plateau, while differences over regional and global conflicts have added to the friction. Given the centrality of both countries to the Quad, the state of their bilateral relationship inevitably shapes the grouping’s broader trajectory.At the same time, the Quad provides a platform through which Washington and New Delhi can sustain cooperation in areas of shared interest even when disagreements persist elsewhere. Critical minerals supply-chain diversification and Indian Ocean security are two examples of overlapping priorities that offer scope for continued engagement.Maintaining these areas of cooperation serves a longer-term purpose, too. It preserves institutional relationships and working-level channels that could facilitate renewed engagement under future U.S. leadership.3. The gap between the Quad’s collective ambitions and bilateral implementation remains pronounced.Despite the announcement of initiatives such as the Indo-Pacific Energy Security Initiative and the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework, much of the substantive progress on shared economic and energy security priorities continues to take place bilaterally rather than through the Quad as a collective.Examples include India-Japan cooperation under the Joint Vision for the Next Decade and India-Australia critical minerals collaboration, alongside bilateral engagement involving the United States and the other Quad partners. By comparison, progress in these areas among all four countries collectively remains more declaratory than operational, with the exception of maritime security.This gap matters because critical minerals security is a shared regional imperative with implications for industrial resilience, clean-energy transitions, and strategic dependencies. The Quad has an opportunity to add value by coordinating complementary bilateral efforts, identifying gaps across supply chains, and establishing practical mechanisms for cooperation.4. Expanding Quad membership is less urgent than deepening cooperation with existing partners and regional institutions.Adding new members to the Quad is unlikely to be productive at this stage. Rather than expanding the grouping’s formal membership, the four countries should pursue issue-specific cooperation with partners whose interests align with Quad priorities. Singapore, Indonesia, and South Korea, for example, could contribute to relevant initiatives in appropriate formats, including through observer-style participation where useful.The experience of BRICS illustrates the potential trade-offs involved in expansion. Adding members with divergent strategic priorities can complicate consensus and dilute a grouping’s sense of purpose, particularly when members disagree over divisive issues such as the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. Any expansion should be guided by a clear strategic rationale and a realistic assessment of what additional members can contribute.For the Quad, a more immediate priority is to make better use of existing regional platforms, including ASEAN, the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA), the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), and the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF). Working through these institutions can broaden regional participation, reinforce local ownership, and create opportunities for tangible cooperation without complicating the Quad’s internal decision-making.5. Southeast Asia’s comfort with the Quad depends in part on its ability to deliver practical public goods and respect ASEAN’s role.In Southeast Asia, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief remain among the areas of Quad engagement that are most readily accepted. Regional governments remain wary of China’s influence, but this does not automatically translate into support for an explicitly competitive or exclusive regional framework. ASEAN also wants to be included in the region’s evolving security architecture and to demonstrate its continued relevance.This creates both an opportunity and an obligation for the Quad. Practical cooperation on disaster response, maritime awareness, and other shared challenges can build confidence while delivering benefits that are visible to regional partners. But these efforts must complement, rather than bypass, ASEAN-led mechanisms and priorities.6. Uncertainty over the Quad’s strategic purpose is compounded by Washington’s approach to China.President Donald Trump’s apparent preference for dealing with China without relying on other countries complicates the Quad’s strategic rationale. If Washington places less emphasis on collective coordination as a means of managing Beijing’s rise, the grouping’s implicit role in balancing Chinese influence becomes harder to sustain.This raises a fundamental question: what is the Quad’s mission if its members do not share a clear understanding of the strategic challenge it is intended to address? The ambiguity has implications beyond the grouping itself. Japan, for example, must navigate its own strained relationship with China while assessing the durability of U.S. engagement. India, meanwhile, must consider how the state of U.S.-China strategic stability could affect its own leverage in Washington.The Quad need not define itself exclusively in opposition to China to remain relevant. However, it does need a clearer shared understanding of its purpose, the challenges it is equipped to address, and the forms of cooperation its members are prepared to sustain.7. Recent crises have exposed the gap between the Quad’s stated priorities and its ability to respond collectively.The ongoing Iran crisis has not seen the Quad activate its maritime security or energy security cooperation in a coordinated manner, despite the relevance of both areas to the grouping’s stated agenda. Similarly, following the floods in Nepal, all four member countries provided humanitarian and disaster relief assistance, but not under the Quad banner.These examples highlight a recurring challenge: the existence of shared capabilities and parallel national efforts does not automatically translate into collective action. Bilateral or independent responses may be entirely appropriate in particular circumstances, but the Quad’s added value should be evident when coordination among the four partners can improve the speed, scale, or effectiveness of a response.8. Japan’s leadership and its partnership with India could become increasingly important to the Quad’s continuity.When the Quad functions effectively, it advances a broad set of Japanese priorities, particularly through its attention to the Indian Ocean and the protection of the sea lanes on which Japan’s economy depends. Japan’s leadership is therefore important to sustaining the grouping, especially if U.S. engagement becomes less consistent.The Japan-India partnership could also become a defining feature of efforts to sustain an Indo-Pacific order grounded in shared rules and principles. Both countries have an interest in regional stability, secure maritime routes, and a framework that preserves space for cooperation among Indo-Pacific states. Deeper coordination between Tokyo and New Delhi could help maintain momentum across the Quad’s agenda.This would not eliminate the importance of U.S. leadership, which remains central to the grouping’s strategic weight. It would, however, give the Quad a broader base from which to sustain cooperation should Washington retrench.AcknowledgementsASPI extends its sincere gratitude to the Japan Foundation for its generous support of this timely and important project on Cementing the Quad in the Indo-Pacific. We are deeply appreciative of the many experts who contributed their time and insights. Their expertise was instrumental to the project’s findings and success.
